questions.stem: The relationship between AI and ML is:
options: All ML is AI, but not all AI is ML
questions.explanation: AI is the broad field of systems simulating human intelligence; ML is the subset that learns from data rather than following explicitly programmed rules. A hand-coded rule-based expert system is AI but not ML.

questions.stem: The DevOps cycle has how many stages?
questions.explanation: 8 — Plan, Develop, Build, Test, Release, Deploy, Operate, Monitor. Automating the middle of that cycle is CI/CD.

questions.stem: The five goals of DevOps are:
options: Speed, automation, CI/CD, collaboration, monitoring and feedback
questions.explanation: The central idea is that development and operations work as one team rather than throwing releases over a wall.

questions.stem: CI/CD stands for:
questions.explanation: An automated pipeline that builds, tests and deploys on every code submission — so defects surface within minutes rather than at a quarterly release.

questions.stem: RPA is best described as:
options: Physical robots on a production line
A machine learning model that improves with data
Software bots automating repetitive, rule-based tasks a human would do on a computer
questions.explanation: RPA clicks buttons, enters data, copies and pastes, reads emails and files. It works with existing software, involves no physical robots, and does not learn.

questions.stem: BPA differs from RPA because BPA:
options: Automates an entire business process, typically spanning multiple departments
questions.explanation: Examples: employee onboarding, customer onboarding with background checks, IT service desk support, marketing automation. RPA automates a task; BPA automates a process.

questions.stem: Which automates the development process itself rather than a business task?
questions.explanation: DevOps — RPA automates a human's computer task, BPA automates a cross-department workflow, DevOps automates building, testing and shipping software.

questions.stem: MLOps exists primarily because:
options: ML models are too small to deploy manually
Models break when the data they see changes over time (data drift), and manual deployment is slow and error-prone
questions.explanation: MLOps adds monitoring of model performance and data drift, versioning of data, weights and training configurations (DVC, MLflow), and ML pipelines (Airflow, Kubeflow).

questions.stem: The three stages of MLOps are:
questions.explanation: Design → Model Development → Operations — MLOps is not an explicit NESA dot point, so use it as evidence of depth on how an ML solution is developed and maintained.

questions.stem: Data drift means:
options: The data a deployed model encounters changes over time, degrading its accuracy
Training data was corrupted during storage
The model's weights are randomly initialised
Data is transferred slowly across the network
questions.explanation: It is why a deployed model is an ongoing operational commitment requiring monitoring and scheduled retraining, not a finished artefact.

questions.stem: MLOps versions which additional artefacts that DevOps typically does not?
options: Data, model weights and training configurations
questions.explanation: Without versioned data and weights, a model result cannot be reproduced — the ML equivalent of losing the source code.

questions.stem: Supervised learning is characterised by:
options: Labelled data — both the input and the correct output are provided during training
Rewards and penalties from an environment
A small amount of labelled data plus a large unlabelled set
questions.explanation: Classification and regression are the two supervised problem types.

questions.stem: Grouping customers by purchasing behaviour with no predefined categories is:
questions.explanation: Unsupervised — the model finds patterns or groupings on its own. Algorithms include K-Means and DBSCAN.

questions.stem: Semi-supervised learning uses:
options: A small amount of labelled data plus a large amount of unlabelled data
questions.explanation: It captures much of supervised learning's accuracy without the cost of labelling everything — labelling is often the most expensive part of an ML project.

questions.stem: Reinforcement learning trains a model by:
options: Having it interact with an environment and adjust behaviour to maximise reward over time
Providing correct answers for every example
questions.explanation: Used in game playing, robotics and dynamic control — problems where the right action is only revealed through consequences.

questions.stem: The exploration versus exploitation trade-off means balancing:
options: Trying new actions to discover better strategies against using known successful strategies to maximise reward
questions.explanation: Pure exploitation locks in a mediocre strategy; pure exploration never cashes in. A good RL agent must do both.

questions.stem: Which analytics type answers "What should we do?"
questions.explanation: Prescriptive — e.g. recommending marketing strategies. Descriptive summarises what happened; predictive forecasts what will happen.

questions.stem: Data wrangling includes all of the following except:
options: Filling missing values with the average or removing them
Choosing the number of hidden layers
Scaling numerical values so large differences are balanced
questions.explanation: that is a model architecture decision, not data preparation. Wrangling also removes duplicates and errors.

questions.stem: Scaling numerical features before training matters because:
options: Features on very different scales, such as salary and age, would otherwise dominate distance and weight calculations
questions.explanation: It is particularly critical for distance-based algorithms such as KNN, where an unscaled salary column would swamp every other feature.

questions.stem: NLP underpins which applications?
questions.explanation: Its named challenges are accents and dialects, and context understanding across a multi-turn conversation.

questions.stem: In image recognition, a multi-layered network typically detects features in which order?
options: Edges → simple shapes → the whole image
questions.explanation: Accuracy depends on the quantity and variety of training data, and the usual architecture is a CNN.

questions.stem: A chatbot raises which named human-behaviour issue?
options: Users need to know they are talking to a machine, with a clear path to a human
questions.explanation: This is the psychological response dot point — trust, transparency and explainability shape design decisions.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: The top node of a decision tree, representing the entire dataset, is the:
questions.explanation: Root node — Internal nodes are decision points on features, branches are paths, and leaf nodes hold the final classification or prediction.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: Pruning a decision tree means:
options: Adding more sub-nodes to increase accuracy
questions.explanation: Over-aggressive pruning causes the opposite failure — underfitting, where the model is too simple to capture the real pattern.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: The Gini index measures:
questions.explanation: Purity — Entropy measures randomness. A pure node contains only one type of outcome.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: A traditional decision tree differs from an ML decision tree because the traditional one is:
options: Trained on historical data and adapts when retrained
A static, rule-based structure set by domain experts that does not adapt
questions.explanation: ML trees learn patterns from data, adapt on retraining, and model non-linear relationships. This comparison is a ready-made "compare and contrast" answer.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: Decision trees can be used for:
questions.explanation: Both — Their standout advantage is interpretability — every path is readable as an IF-THEN rule, which matters where a decision must be explained.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: In a neural network's input layer, each neuron represents:
options: One feature of the input data
questions.explanation: One feature — The output layer produces the prediction — with many possibilities, each output neuron gives a probability and the highest is chosen.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: A neuron computes its output by:
options: Summing each input multiplied by its weight, adding a bias, then applying an activation function
questions.explanation: Each node is effectively its own linear regression model composed of inputs, weights, a bias and an output.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: Inputs x₁ = 0.8, x₂ = 0.3 with weights w₁ = 0.5, w₂ = 0.9 and bias 0.1 produce a weighted sum of:
questions.explanation: 0.77 — (0.8 × 0.5) + (0.3 × 0.9) + 0.1 = 0.4 + 0.27 + 0.1 = 0.77, which is then passed through the activation function.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: The bias in a neuron is equivalent to which part of y = mx + b?
questions.explanation: The y-intercept — The weight corresponds to the slope. Both are parameters learned during training.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: An activation function exists to:
options: Determine whether and how strongly a neuron fires, mapping the weighted sum into a bounded range
questions.explanation: Commonly a sigmoid, producing an S-shaped output between 0 and 1 — the same function used in logistic regression.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: Gradient descent is the process by which a model:
options: Adjusts its weights and biases in the direction that reduces error, minimising the cost function
Splits data into training and test sets
questions.explanation: The cost function is the measure of error being minimised.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: A CNN is typically used for:
questions.explanation: Image recognition — An RNN, identified by its feedback loops, is used for sequential prediction such as sales forecasting.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: Deep learning refers to:
options: Neural networks with more hidden layers, combining input data in more complex ways
Any use of a neural network
Learning from very large images only
questions.explanation: The costs are computational expense and reduced interpretability — the deeper the network, the harder it becomes for people to explain a decision.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: A hidden layer in a neural network:
options: Performs computations and transformations between the input and output layers
questions.explanation: More hidden layers = a deeper network capable of representing more complex relationships.

questions.stem: In y' = b + w₁x₁, w₁ represents:
options: The weight — the feature's importance, equivalent to the slope
questions.explanation: Weight — y' is the predicted label, b is the bias (y-intercept), x₁ is the feature. Multiple features extend it: y' = b + w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + w₃x₃ …

questions.stem: Logistic regression is used for:
options: Binary classification — the output is one of two values
questions.explanation: Despite its name it is a classification algorithm — a classic multiple-choice trap. It uses a sigmoid to output a probability 0–1, thresholded at typically 0.5.

questions.stem: Which is the correct threshold value normally used with logistic regression?
questions.explanation: 0.5 — A probability at or above the threshold is assigned to class 1. The threshold can be tuned when false positives and false negatives have different costs.

questions.stem: Predicting house prices from size and location is best served by:
questions.explanation: Linear regression — a continuous numeric output. XGBoost is also named for regression problems.

questions.stem: KNN classifies a new data point by:
options: Fitting a line of best fit
Taking the majority class of the k closest existing points
Splitting on the feature with the lowest Gini index
questions.explanation: Its assumption is that similar points are located near each other, which is why feature scaling and the choice of distance metric matter so much.

questions.stem: KNN's two hyperparameters are:
options: A distance metric and the value of K
questions.explanation: They are hyperparameters — chosen by the developer before training — unlike weights and biases, which the model learns.

questions.stem: K in KNN should generally be an odd number because:
options: It avoids ties in the majority vote
questions.explanation: Data with more outliers benefits from a larger K, which smooths the decision boundary; very low K overfits.

questions.stem: KNN is called a lazy algorithm because it:
options: Stores all training data and defers computation until classification time
questions.explanation: The consequences are high memory use and slow prediction — it "doesn't scale well".

questions.stem: The curse of dimensionality describes KNN's weakness with:
questions.explanation: As dimensions increase, points become nearly equidistant and "nearest neighbour" stops carrying meaning.

questions.stem: Which is the correct pairing of problem type and common algorithm?
questions.explanation: Classification → decision trees, random forest, neural networks. Regression → linear regression, XGBoost. Clustering → K-Means, DBSCAN. Deep learning → neural networks, Transformers (BERT, GPT).

questions.stem: KNN and K-Means differ because:
options: KNN is supervised classification using labelled neighbours; K-Means is unsupervised clustering finding groups in unlabelled data
K-Means requires labels; KNN does not
KNN produces clusters; K-Means produces classes
questions.explanation: A named adjacent-term trap — the shared "K" is coincidental, and they solve opposite kinds of problem.

questions.stem: Overfitting is best described as a model that:
options: Has learned specific details and noise rather than generalisable patterns
Is too simple to capture the pattern
questions.explanation: It scores very well on training data and poorly on unseen data. Underfitting is the opposite failure — poor on both.

questions.stem: The reason a model must be evaluated on unseen test data is:
options: Evaluating on data the model has already seen hides overfitting, since a memorising model scores perfectly on it
questions.explanation: The labelled set is split — the model learns from the training data and is judged on the test data.

questions.stem: A hyperparameter differs from a parameter because a hyperparameter is:
options: Learned by the model during training
Chosen by the developer before training begins
questions.explanation: Weights and biases are parameters learned during training; K, the distance metric and the number of hidden layers are hyperparameters set beforehand.

questions.stem: In an OOP implementation of a neural network, a Layer class would most sensibly:
questions.explanation: The output of one layer becomes the input to the next — composition mirrors the network's actual structure.

questions.stem: In Python, __init__ is:
options: A method called manually after object creation
The constructor, which runs automatically when an object is created
questions.explanation: self refers to the specific object the method is called on, distinguishing instance data from class-level data.

questions.stem: In OOP, a class and an object relate as:
options: A class is the blueprint; an object is a specific instance of it
A class is a specific instance of an object
questions.explanation: Attributes are the object's data; methods are its behaviour.

questions.stem: super().__init__() is used to:
options: Call the parent class's constructor from a subclass
questions.explanation: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and extend a parent class — shown on a class diagram by a hollow triangle arrow pointing from subclass to parent.

questions.stem: The key difference between procedural and object-oriented programming is:
options: Procedural treats data and procedures as separate entities; OOP bundles data and behaviour together in objects
questions.explanation: OOP's advantage in an ML context is that a Neuron naturally has weights and a bias and does a forward pass.

questions.stem: In the NESA locked-down Python editor, which library is available?
questions.explanation: math — Standard library only — math, random, os and datetime. No NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, SciPy, scikit-learn, Requests, OpenCV or Tkinter, and no internet.

questions.stem: Implementing a regression model without external libraries means you must:
options: Calculate the weighted sum and update weights with plain arithmetic and loops
questions.explanation: Exam questions on "programming an ML model" are testing your ability to express the maths in code, not to call a library.

questions.stem: Which Python structure is immutable?
questions.explanation: tuple — A list is ordered and mutable, a dict holds key–value pairs, and a set is unordered with unique values only.

questions.stem: A for loop is described as definite iteration because:
options: It always runs at least once
It runs faster than a while loop
The number of repetitions is known in advance
questions.explanation: A while loop is indefinite — it repeats until a condition becomes false, which may be an unknown number of times.

questions.stem: To modify a global variable inside a function in Python you must:
questions.explanation: Reading a global works without the keyword; modifying it requires global. Heavy reliance on globals is a maintainability problem in its own right.

questions.stem: Which is a documented negative of automation for worker safety?
options: New human–robot collaboration hazards, as in the Tesla case study — malfunctioning machines, injuries and insufficient emergency stop mechanisms
questions.explanation: Tesla is the ready-made counterexample to "automation improves workplace safety" — overly complex automation caused delays, breakdowns and injuries.

questions.stem: Automation's effect on employment is best characterised as:
options: Repetitive roles displaced, new roles created in AI training, oversight and maintenance, and existing roles requiring upskilling
questions.explanation: Every impact dimension is two-sided — if the verb is discuss, assess or evaluate, both sides are required.

questions.stem: According to the figures in the school notes, approximately what proportion of global employment is exposed to AI?
questions.explanation: ~40% — globally — about 60% in advanced economies, 40% in emerging markets and 26% in low-income countries. Roughly half the exposed roles may benefit from AI integration; the other half may see lower labour demand.

questions.stem: The environmental case against large-scale automation centres on:
options: Significant energy and water consumption from training large models and running data centres
questions.explanation: Balance it against efficiency gains and reduced material waste, then make a judgement.

questions.stem: The equity concern about automation and the economy is that:
options: Benefits may concentrate among owners of automated systems rather than displaced workers
questions.explanation: Distribution, not aggregate output, is the contested point — which is what makes it an ethical rather than purely economic question.

questions.stem: Automation affects people with disability in which two-sided way?
options: Positively through accessibility tools, but negatively where systems are not designed inclusively and exclude users
Only positively, through speech-to-text and captioning
questions.explanation: Automated captioning and speech-to-text expand independence; an inaccessible automated kiosk removes a service that a human counter previously provided.

questions.stem: Designing an AI system for use by emergency services must account for the acute stress response, meaning:
options: Under fight/flight/freeze conditions, systems must minimise cognitive load, give real-time feedback, adapt, and use calming language
Users will read long instructions carefully
questions.explanation: Human behaviour under stress is a design input, not an afterthought — a fact worth naming explicitly in an extended response.

questions.stem: Cultural protocols in AI development specifically include:
options: Data sovereignty regarding data about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities — who controls it, who may access it, and for what purpose
questions.explanation: Data sovereignty here means data is subject to the laws and cultural governance of the place and people it comes from.

questions.stem: How do belief systems influence ML development?
options: They set the number of hidden layers
Differing values affect what users consider acceptable automation, such as attitudes to AI in healthcare decision-making
questions.explanation: It sits alongside psychological responses, acute stress response and cultural protocols in the human-behaviour dot points.

questions.stem: The four sources of bias in ML are:
options: Data, algorithmic, human decision, generative AI
questions.explanation: Data bias comes from unrepresentative training data; algorithmic bias from design and parameters; human decision bias from subjective choices in labelling and development; generative AI bias from models producing stereotyped content.

questions.stem: Algorithmic bias can arise:
options: Only when the data is biased
Even when the data itself is unbiased, through how features are processed and prioritised
questions.explanation: Which is why fixing the dataset is necessary but not sufficient — feature selection, weighting and thresholds all encode choices.

questions.stem: The four bias mitigation strategies are:
options: Data pre-processing, fairness-aware algorithms, data post-processing, auditing and transparency
questions.explanation: Name the stage each operates at — before training, during training, after inference, and continuously.

questions.stem: A recruitment screening model trained on a decade of hiring data systematically downgraded women's applications. This illustrates:
options: Dataset bias — historical data from a male-dominated industry taught the model to treat maleness as a marker of success
questions.explanation: No explicit rule was written; the pattern existed in the data. It shows how a system that appears neutral and purely data-driven still reproduces and amplifies unfairness.

questions.stem: The most significant consequence of biased ML outputs is:
options: Poor and unfair performance for underrepresented groups, eroding trust in the system as a reliable source of information
questions.explanation: The 2025 marker feedback specifically rewarded answers that used stimulus examples to identify bias categories and then explained the broader effect on usefulness, rather than restating the stimulus.

questions.stem: Explainability features are added to automated decision systems primarily because:
options: Users' psychological responses — whether they trust or distrust automated decisions — determine whether the system is used and accepted
They are required by the W3C
questions.explanation: An accurate model nobody trusts or acts on has failed on the criterion that matters.

questions.stem: A dataset has 200 labelled examples and 12 features, and the client needs to explain every decision to a regulator. The best model choice is:
options: A decision tree, because it is interpretable and does not need a large dataset
questions.explanation: Justify with both reasons: interpretability for the regulator, and the fact that 200 examples cannot train a deep network without severe overfitting. Saying why not a neural network is where the mark sits.

questions.stem: A model achieves 99% accuracy on training data and 61% on test data. The diagnosis and remedy are:
options: Overfitting; simplify the model, prune, or gather more and more varied training data
questions.explanation: The gap between training and test performance is the signature of overfitting.

questions.stem: A spam filter's accuracy falls steadily over six months. The most likely cause is:
options: Data drift — spam tactics changed, so the deployed model no longer matches the data it sees
questions.explanation: The MLOps response is monitoring for drift plus scheduled retraining, with versioned data and weights so results remain reproducible.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants to automate copying invoice data between two legacy systems that have no API. The correct technology is:
questions.explanation: RPA — It works with existing software exactly as a human would, which is its whole value proposition where integration is impossible.

questions.stem: Automating employee onboarding across HR, IT and payroll is:
questions.explanation: BPA — a business process spanning multiple departments, as opposed to a single repetitive task.

questions.stem: A team deploys a model by manually copying files to a server every few weeks. The best improvement is:
options: An MLOps pipeline automating training, validation, deployment and monitoring, with versioned data and weights
questions.explanation: Manual deployment is slow and error-prone, and without versioning a regression cannot be traced to a cause.

questions.stem: Which statement about a neural network's interpretability is most accurate?
options: Interpretability decreases as depth increases, which is a genuine limitation where decisions must be justified
Interpretability depends only on the training data
questions.explanation: This is precisely why a simpler interpretable model is often the better engineering choice in regulated or high-stakes contexts.

questions.stem: Predicting whether a transaction is fraudulent (yes/no) is a:
questions.explanation: Classification — Suitable algorithms: logistic regression, decision trees, random forest, neural networks.

questions.stem: A model that must run on a device with no internet connection favours:
options: KNN storing the entire training set
A small, efficient model such as a decision tree or compact network deployed on-device
questions.explanation: KNN is a poor fit precisely because it is lazy — it must carry all training data with it and computes at prediction time.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest evidence that an automation project succeeded?
options: The team used the newest framework
A measured improvement in the target business metric against a pre-implementation baseline, with the model's ongoing accuracy monitored
questions.explanation: Define the metric and baseline before deployment, or evaluation becomes an argument rather than a measurement.

questions.stem: A model is trained on data collected only from one metropolitan area and deployed nationally. The predictable failure is:
options: Poor performance and unfair outcomes for populations unlike the training distribution
questions.explanation: It is dataset bias caused by an unrepresentative sample — the mitigation is representative data collection plus post-deployment auditing by subgroup.

questions.stem: A team removes the "gender" field so their model "cannot be biased". The best critique is:
options: The model needs gender to be accurate
Bias only occurs in neural networks
Proxy features — suburb, school, career gaps, hobbies — can reconstruct the attribute, so removing the field does not remove the bias
questions.explanation: Fairness must be tested on outcomes across groups, not asserted from the absence of an input.

questions.stem: A supervised model's labels were assigned by a single annotator applying their own judgement. The bias source is:
questions.explanation: Mitigate with multiple annotators, measured inter-rater agreement, documented labelling guidelines and auditing.

questions.stem: In a CI/CD pipeline, automated tests run:
options: Only when a developer requests them
On every code submission, so defects are caught within minutes of introduction
questions.explanation: This is the practical mechanism behind DevOps's goals of speed and feedback.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches an algorithm to its output type?
options: Logistic regression → a probability that is thresholded into one of two classes
questions.explanation: Linear regression → a continuous numeric value. KNN → a class. K-Means → unlabelled clusters.

questions.stem: A decision tree is 40 levels deep and perfectly classifies the training data. The appropriate action is:
options: Prune it, because that depth indicates it has memorised noise rather than learned patterns
Convert it to a neural network
questions.explanation: Perfect training accuracy is a warning sign, not an achievement.

questions.stem: The main reason an organisation would choose semi-supervised learning is:
options: Labelling is expensive, so a small labelled set plus a large unlabelled set captures much of the benefit at lower cost
questions.explanation: Labelling is often the largest single cost in an ML project.

questions.stem: A VPA repeatedly misinterprets a user with a regional accent. This illustrates:
options: An NLP challenge and a dataset representativeness problem, producing unequal service quality
questions.explanation: Named NLP challenges are accents and dialects, privacy and security, and context understanding across a multi-turn conversation.

questions.stem: Which is the most defensible order of activity for an automation project?
options: Choose the algorithm → find a problem → collect data
Train → define the problem → wrangle data
Deploy → collect data → define the problem
Define the problem and success metric → collect and wrangle data → select and train a model → evaluate on unseen data → deploy → monitor and retrain
questions.explanation: Technology-led adoption — picking a model first and hunting for a use case — is the most common and most expensive failure pattern.

questions.stem: Automating a decision that materially affects a person requires, at minimum:
options: Human oversight, an explanation of the decision, and a route to review or appeal
questions.explanation: This is where explainability, psychological response and ethical accountability converge — and where an interpretable model may be worth an accuracy trade.

questions.stem: In a stimulus question about bias, the highest-scoring approach is to:
options: Use specific examples from the stimulus to identify the bias categories present, then explain the broader effect on the system's usefulness and fairness
questions.explanation: Direct 2025 marker feedback: don't just restate the stimulus — explain its implications.

questions.stem: Which claim about automation is not supported by the module?
options: Automation guarantees improved workplace safety in all cases
Automation can remove humans from dangerous tasks
Automation can concentrate economic benefit among system owners
Automation can exclude people if systems are not designed inclusively
questions.explanation: The Tesla case study directly contradicts it. Every impact dot point has a documented counterexample — which is what makes them examinable as "discuss".

questions.stem: The best justification for using a random forest rather than a single decision tree is:
options: Combining many trees reduces overfitting and usually improves accuracy, at the cost of interpretability
questions.explanation: The trade-off is exactly the one that runs through this whole module — accuracy against explainability.

questions.stem: A model is evaluated only on the data it was trained on and reports 100% accuracy. The correct response is:
options: Reject the result — it measures memorisation, not generalisation; hold out unseen test data and re-evaluate
questions.explanation: Evaluating on seen data hides overfitting entirely, which is the whole reason for the train/test split.

questions.stem: The strongest concluding judgement in an 8-mark question on automation:
options: "Judged against efficiency gain, workplace safety and equity, the automation is justified for this warehouse — throughput rises and workers are removed from the hazardous picking zone — but the Tesla precedent shows over-automation introduces new human–robot hazards, and the productivity benefit accrues to the owner rather than the displaced pickers, so the recommendation is conditional on retraining commitments and independently audited emergency-stop coverage."
questions.explanation: Criteria stated, both sides weighed with concrete evidence, a conditional judgement made. That structure works for every impact question in this module.
